A dangerous wave of denialism is undermining efforts to secure truth justice, and non-recurrence worldwide. State politicians and other actors are denying past violations, glorifying perpetrators, stigmatizing victims, and erasing collective memory through attacks on civil society and memorialization initiatives. There can be no regression or reversal The denial of genocides, crimes against humanity, and war crimes must be unequivocally rejected and countered. In my last report to the 63rd session of the Human Rights Council, I reflected yesterday on a shift from evidence-based accountability in political discourse which is now replaced with emotionally charged narratives, identity affirmation, and polarization that serve narrow political or ideological interests. Denial of past events is often accompanied by silencing of dissenting voices. It limits understanding of past violence undermine victims' rights to justice and reparations, and it weakens prospects for non-recurrence. Regrettably, too often states respond to denialism through memory or security laws, which have also been problematic, serving as a pretext for censorship and the imposition of a single state-sanctioned narrative. I'm recalling that international law requires the affirmative disclosure of accurate accounts of past violations to ensure maximum transparency, and states should disclose all this information to also ensure accountability, of course. Information concerning international crimes must never be subject to secrecy, classification, or other access restrictions that do not comply with international human rights standards. In fact, freedom of expression, cultural rights, education, and access to knowledge are the most effective tools to counter denialism. Rather than restrictive legislation, states should invest in inclusive, evidence-based, education, critical thinking, digital literacy, and robust memorialization processes. Digital technologies, social media, and artificial intelligence systems have also amplified the scope, reach, and monetization of denialist content. So I call on technology companies to redouble their efforts to ensure regular human rights due diligence and review. Technology companies must act with heightened diligence to avoid fueling denialism, disinformation, and hate speech. And to do so, they must ensure transparency, address business models that incentivize denialist content, and ensure remedies to ensure that their platforms are safe for marginalized persons or groups, as well as, of course, strengthening cooperation with civil society organizations.
